messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Clergy/Pastor
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Affective Expression: Crying, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Hopelessness: I have no future, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
Anjali Rao is a 47-year-old South Asian American pastor who came to treatment after months of telling herself that she should be able to endure this silently. She is divorced and lives alone, and much of her week is spent in the church where she leads services, visits parishioners, and sits with people in crisis. What she has struggled to say plainly, even in therapy, is that she was tortured, and that the experience has not settled into the past in any coherent way. When she tries to describe what happened, the memory does not unfold like a story. Instead, there are isolated flashes that come with painful sharpness—a particular face leaning close, the sensation of being watched, a taste in her mouth she still cannot bear—while whole stretches are blank. She knows there are missing sections, and the gaps disturb her almost as much as the moments she can remember clearly.

Certain details from the torture have stayed lodged in her body. The strongest is gustatory: a specific taste associated with the event can bring her back immediately, before she has time to think. If that taste appears unexpectedly in food or drink, she feels her body surge into alarm at once. She does not experience this as remembering in any ordinary sense; it is more that her body reacts before her mind has caught up. She has tried to explain that even when she is standing in the church kitchen after a committee meeting, surrounded by familiar people, she can suddenly feel as if safety is impossible to trust. Other people may tell her she is safe now, but she finds that impossible to believe in those moments. She becomes acutely watchful, scanning faces, posture, tone, trying to determine whether someone around her is dangerous.

Other triggers are social and emotionally disorienting. Seeing someone cry can affect her unexpectedly. During pastoral work, tears are common, and she has begun dreading the moments when a congregant breaks down in her office or at the altar rail. The sight of crying can pull her toward disconnected fragments of her own ordeal, and she has to work hard to keep herself composed. Talking about what happened is also a trigger in itself. She has learned that the mere act of recounting it can leave her overwhelmed by jagged pieces of memory and intense guilt. When recall begins, what floods in is not only fear but a crushing sense that she did something wrong, though she struggles to say exactly what. She is left feeling ashamed for surviving, ashamed for not remembering more, ashamed for what the event seems to have made of her.

Over time, her life has narrowed around efforts to keep herself steady. One of the most noticeable changes has been around eating. Because the taste linked to the torture can set off such a violent internal reaction, she has become rigid and controlling with food. She eats a very limited range of things, prepared in predictable ways, and experiences this strictness not as preference but as necessity, one of the few areas where she can still exert control. In the church, where meals are woven into community life, this has become harder to hide. She avoids potlucks, declines parishioners’ home-cooked dishes, and invents reasons not to stay for receptions after services. People have noticed her distance, though few understand it.

She also spends much of her time monitoring other people. In meetings, in hallways, after worship, she tracks who is entering, who is lingering, whose expression changes. She knows this level of watchfulness is exhausting, but she feels she cannot stop. Alongside that, she tries to force the trauma from her mind altogether. If thoughts of it begin to surface, she pushes them away quickly because she has come to believe that if she lets herself think about the event fully, she will not be able to handle it. So she keeps busy, redirects herself, shortens conversations, and avoids any setting in which someone might ask directly about her past.

The cost has become increasingly painful to her. She has long understood herself as someone able to sit calmly with suffering, to speak with conviction, to offer spiritual steadiness to others. Now she fears she is no longer capable of the things that defined her. She still performs her role, but with growing dread and a private sense of fraudulence. There are moments after services, when she has successfully preached and greeted everyone, that she returns to her office and feels only emptiness. At her lowest points she has thought, with a flat certainty, that she has no future beyond enduring one day at a time in this diminished state.

What finally brought Anjali to seek help was a recent pastoral meeting in which a parishioner began to cry while describing a family crisis. Anjali felt her body react instantly; she became flooded, lost track of the conversation, and afterward had to lock her office door and sit in silence, afraid to eat, afraid to think, afraid to speak about why. That episode frightened her because it happened in the very setting where she has always known who she is. She has come to treatment wanting some way to live without being ambushed by taste, tears, and conversation, but what frightens her most is the possibility that if she lets the memories come any closer, they will prove she is as broken and incapable as she already fears.
